To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the most effective interventions for addressing undernutrition in children and pregnant and lactating women are known, 2) the most effective actions for addressing undernutrition are known, 3) the most effective strategies for addressing undernutrition have been identified, 4) there are many examples of countries that have successfully addressed undernutrition, and 5) there is a wealth of information about the actions needed to address undernutrition.
the countries with the greatest number of undernourished women and children have not yet achieved a high enough priority for nutrition, and have not yet implemented proven interventions at scale.

in countries with the highest rates of undernutrition there is an urgent need for action to improve the nutritional status of mothers and children, and this can be achieved through the rapid implementation of interventions that have been shown to be effective, and the avoidance of interventions that have not been shown to be beneficial.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the question of how to accelerate the implementation and scale-up of effective nutrition interventions in the 20 high burden countries, and how to ensure that the interventions reach the intended population groups.
how to make the most effective and efficient use of resources in countries to reduce the burden of maternal and child undernutrition.

identifying what is needed to achieve the first MDG and the targets of MDGs 4 and5 in countries with high levels of undernutrition, and with identifying the key elements for success in addressing undernutrition in such countries.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the countries most in need of effective nutrition action are not doing enough of the right things, and are doing too much of the wrong things.
the most effective way to address the challenge of undernutrition is to act at scale, in the most effective way possible.
there are proven effective interventions for reducing undernutrition in the 20 countries with the highest rates of undernutrition.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the most important challenge is not the lack of effective interventions, but the lack of commitment to implement them at scale.
we need to get the right things on our list of priorities, keep them on the list, and do them right.
the world has the knowledge, tools, and resources to end maternal and child undernutrition. The challenge is to use them effectively
The main takeaway from our work is that
countries can achieve rapid reductions in undernutrition if they focus their attention on the seven key challenges and take action to address them.

the world's poorest countries can achieve major improvements in the nutritional status of mothers and children, but only by making the right choices and by implementing those choices with sufficient scale.
the countries with the largest burden of undernutrition can make significant progress towards the first MDG if they take the right actions, at scale, and in a timely fashion.
